assertions.text: Fulfillment method splitting is represented as its own table — items with different fulfillment types (store pickup vs home delivery) cannot share a shipment.
assertions.evidence: Response includes dedicated 'Fulfillment-Type Split' section with its own table showing scenarios where different fulfillment types force splits.

assertions.text: Delivery address splitting is represented as its own table — items going to different addresses must be in separate shipments.
assertions.evidence: 'Delivery-Address Split' section has its own table demonstrating address-based shipment splitting.

assertions.text: Availability splitting is represented as its own table — in-stock items ship immediately, backordered/pre-ordered items ship when available.
assertions.evidence: 'Availability-Window Split' table shows scenarios where items split based on stock/backorder/pre-order status with different ship dates.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation (minimising shipments) is represented as its own table — choosing which warehouses to ship from to minimise total shipment count.
assertions.evidence: 'Warehouse Assignment (Minimise Locations)' section has dedicated table with scenarios showing minimization logic.

assertions.text: Companion product grouping is represented as its own table — paired items (e.g. camera body and lens) should ship together from the same location when possible.
assertions.evidence: 'Companion Co-location' section with dedicated table covering camera body + lens pairing scenarios.

assertions.text: Fulfillment table covers at least: all items for home delivery, all items for store pickup, and a mix of delivery and pickup items.
assertions.evidence: Scenarios include 'All home delivery', 'All store pickup', 'One pickup, one delivery', 'Two delivery, one pickup'.

assertions.text: Delivery address table covers at least: all items to the same address, and items to different addresses.
assertions.evidence: Scenarios: 'All same address', 'Two different addresses', plus 'Multiple items group by matching address' and 'Three different addresses'.

assertions.text: Availability table covers at least: all items in stock, a mix of in-stock and pre-order/backorder, and two backordered/pre-ordered items with different dates. Pre-order and backorder are recognised as equivalent for splitting semantics.
assertions.evidence: Covers: 'All in stock', 'In-stock and pre-order', 'Same backorder date consolidates', 'Different backorder dates split', 'In-stock + two different backorders'—treats pre-order and backorder identically.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table covers at least: single warehouse has full quantity, multi-warehouse split needed, fewer-warehouse split preferred over more warehouses, and cannot fulfill (insufficient total stock).
assertions.evidence: Scenarios: 'One warehouse covers all', 'One warehouse preferred when...', 'Two warehouses needed', 'Two-location option preferred over three', 'Three locations needed', 'Cannot fulfil'.

assertions.text: Companion table covers at least: single warehouse has both companions, unavoidable split (no warehouse has both but both are available), and fulfillment not possible (one companion not available anywhere).
assertions.evidence: Covers single warehouse with both and unavoidable split, but no scenario where one companion is out of stock everywhere (e.g. 'Camera lens unavailable, body available').

assertions.text: Scenario names describe the business situation (e.g. 'Consolidate: two beats three', 'Everything at one warehouse') — not 'Test case 2'.
assertions.evidence: Scenarios use descriptive names like 'All home delivery', 'One warehouse covers all', 'Two-location option preferred over three', 'Fulfillment type overrides companion preference'.

assertions.text: Trigger tables represent multi-item orders where each item has its own fulfillment type, address, and availability. The notation makes the item-to-property mapping unambiguous — not value sets like {delivery, pickup}.
assertions.evidence: Uses positional list mapping: 'Shirt, Jacket' paired with 'Delivery, Pickup' is unambiguous (position 1→1, 2→2); output confirms with 'Shirt + Jacket → Home'.

assertions.text: Warehouse allocation table uses a scalar count column (e.g. 'Qty ordered') not item lists, when product identity doesn't matter for the logic.
assertions.evidence: Column labeled 'Item + Qty' with values 'Shirt ×6', 'Shirt ×6', etc. includes product identity ('Shirt') in every row despite it not varying—should omit product name for scalar count.

assertions.text: Column names use business/domain language (e.g. 'Shipments?' not 'Result?', 'Warehouse stock' not 'inventory_map'). The tables read as a specification a product person could review.
assertions.evidence: Columns use 'Fulfillment Types', 'Delivery Addresses', 'Warehouse Stock', 'Shipments?', 'Locations Used?', 'Co-located?'—all business-friendly.

assertions.text: Output/expected columns end with '?' (e.g. 'Shipments?', 'Groups?') to distinguish them from input columns.
assertions.evidence: All output columns use '?': 'Shipments?', 'Shipment 1?', 'Locations Used?', 'Assignment?', 'Co-located?'; input columns have no '?'.

assertions.text: Inventory assignments are physically valid: items are only assigned to locations that have them. Shipment counts match the assignments shown.
assertions.evidence: E.g., 'Two warehouses needed': Shirt ×6 with Philadelphia: 3, Washington: 3 → assigns Philadelphia ×3, Washington ×3 (6 total, both available).

assertions.text: Multiple open questions are surfaced across the tables — ambiguities, edge cases, or product decisions that the requirements don't fully specify.
assertions.evidence: Three open questions included: availability window tolerance (Monday vs Thursday), tie-breaking for equal warehouse combinations, and waiting behavior for backordered companions.

assertions.text: Multiple tables (or @TableTest methods) are used, each addressing a distinct concern — not one monolithic table mixing unrelated rules.
assertions.evidence: Five separate tables: Fulfillment-Type Split, Availability-Window Split, Delivery-Address Split, Warehouse Assignment, Companion Co-location—each addresses one concern.

assertions.text: Each table has only the rows needed to express its concern's rules — no unnecessary permutations from combining concerns. Fewer rows per table is expected when concerns are properly separated.
assertions.evidence: Fulfillment (4 rows), Availability (5 rows), Address (4 rows), Warehouse (6 rows), Companion (6 rows)—each minimal for its concern without cross-concern cartesian expansion.
